utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, lest I run any risk, I would kindly ask that the witness be allowed to leave the courtroom for a second. Or he can take off his headphones. I don't know if he understand English. And also I don't know whether he can hear the interpretation even if he takes his headphones off.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. And you have considered that what you want to tell us is really important enough to ask the witness to leave the courtroom?

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, I will try to simplify matters. The witness is an operative with a great deal of experience who wrote and read many, many documents. I wanted to hear his understanding of the document. Also, as a person whose mother tongue is B/C/S, or, rather, the Serbian language, from a linguistic point of view could he describe specifically the word "susreo."

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: "Met." Interpreter's note.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] That is why I put this question to the witness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. That's clear, and you may proceed. And you're still invited to focus very much on facts rather than -- not to say that it's useless to hear from someone who has read many reports. At the same time, it is -- if -- of any assistance, of limited assistance. So please focus on the facts.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, just one more question in relation to this document. And after that I'm not going to go back to the document.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Mr. Novakovic, in the second and third paragraphs of this document there is also reference to some encounters that the author of the document had with certain individuals. Is an operative of the service expected to do the following: If these encounters were meaningful, is an operative of the service expected to write this up in an official note if he talked to these persons and what these persons said and what was discussed?

utterances.speaker: RADENKO NOVAKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Absolutely. If an operative has contacts, on the ground in particular, he's expected to say what kind of contact it was and what was discussed.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Novakovic. While we are -- actually, we're not in private session.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, could we briefly move into private session, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: We move into private session.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: We're in private session, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you, Madam Registrar.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honour. D784, could would have a look at that again, please.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Mr. Novakovic, it's not very legible, but I believe that you have a hard copy in front of you. A few moments ago you read it.

utterances.speaker: RADENKO NOVAKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Can you explain to us why this document is being sent along a different line of work -- or, rather, the second line of work? Why is it being sent along that line of work? What is so characteristic about it?

utterances.speaker: RADENKO NOVAKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, the content of the document is a portrayal of the current situation as the session of the Assembly of Republika Srpska was being held in Sanski Most, and it shows the active clash that took place between the military and political leadership at that point in time.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: The information contained in this report, what type of information is this? What nature does this information have?

utterances.speaker: RADENKO NOVAKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It is intelligence, absolutely.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Novakovic. And just one more question. Perhaps it hasn't been clarified fully. You mentioned that there was a conflict between Milan Lukic and the family of Mihajlo Lukic. What kind of relationship did they have? Or, rather, what led to this conflict, and what was their relationship between Milan and Mihajlo?

utterances.speaker: RADENKO NOVAKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm sorry, I tried to explain the difference between Mihajlo and Milan Lukic. When Milan Lukic stayed in the area of Visegrad --

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Please slow down so that this can be recorded.

utterances.speaker: RADENKO NOVAKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: In terms of the reasons, as Mihajlo Lukic said to me, one of the reasons why his uncle had been killed in the village where Mihajlo's father and uncle lived, as far as I can remember the man was wounded near the house of a man who hadn't been a combatant at all. This was probably done on the basis of some revenge, and he bled to death. I know that Mihajlo Lukic never liked the fact that Milan Lukic was in the area of Visegrad. And ultimately he was convicted, because the family, the father of Mihajlo Lukic, lived in the area of Republika Srpska throughout.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Mr. Novakovic, again it is not clear. What was it that Mihajlo Lukic said to you was one of the reasons for the killing of his uncle?

utterances.speaker: RADENKO NOVAKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: He thought that one of the reasons was precisely that, the fact that Milan Lukic was staying in the territory of Visegrad. And what he had committed there. I'm saying this to you on the basis of what I remember. I remember that Mihajlo was very bitter at the time.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Do I understand you correctly: Mihajlo believes that the death of his uncle is revenge for what Milan Lukic did?

utterances.speaker: RADENKO NOVAKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: He didn't specifically say that it was revenge, but that certainly contributed to it. I cannot remember what year it was exactly.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Mr. Novakovic. Thank you, Your Honours. I have no further questions.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Petrovic. I'm seeking one clarification of one of your answers. It relates to the previous document. If you'd like to have it on the screen, then we'll put it on the screen. I think it's 3169. That's the document in which the meeting at the hotel was mentioned and the encounter at -- in the days following this first, as you said, see Lukic in passing. Now, in relation to a question put to you by Mr. Petrovic, you told us the following: "If these encounters were meaningful, as an operative of the service expected to write this up in an Official Note if he talked to these persons and what these persons said and what was discussed?" And you said: Absolutely. If an operative has contact, on the grounds in particular, he was expected to say who was contacted and what was discussed. Now, in the question there was a suggestion that perhaps such information was not in this document because there may have been no conversation at all. Is that how you understand the document, or do you think that there has been a conversation during these encounters?

utterances.speaker: RADENKO NOVAKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I personally think that there hadn't been any contact. Look, this term that is used in our language, "met," that means that -- when we would meet. But "susreo," as opposed to "sreo," would be to see in passing.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I was focusing also on the encounters which are described: I encountered the same group dressed in the same manner 10 to 15 days later in the operations to liberate Zepa during the encounter with this group in Bratunac and Srebrenica. Lukic Mihajlo, an operative were present. Now, these encounters, do you understand this report to be that there has been any exchange of information or any conversation, or is it your understanding that that did not take place?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, let me tell you. From this point of view, as I'm giving a comment in respect of the way it was written here, I'm not in a position to say that there had been meetings and contacts. However, they say that during their stay they met these persons that they refer to in this note. Whether they talked to these persons about anything, I don't know. I'm not in a position to comment on that. But had there been any contact, talks between them, I believe that they would have written that up.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. How do you interpret that last line of the second page of this document? Could we move, in the English translation, to the second page. And we need to have a look whether it's on the first page in B/C/S. If we could move it a little bit -- no, second -- could we have a look at the original. No. One second. Yes. It's still the first page. It says: "Lukic Mihajlo, an operative of Uzice SDB, was informed about this." How would he have been informed?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Could you please show the document to me so that I could see? I mean, I have the English version here, but not --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: For the witness, the B/C/S version, please. Last lines.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The last sentence: Radivojevic and Nakarada managed to flee from Bratunac to the FRY. Mihajlo Lukic, an operative of the SDB Uzice, was made aware of this. This is how I understand this: That Lukic knew that the two mentioned persons fled from Bratunac to the FRY, and I assume that he informed someone about that. I don't know. The persons in the centre who were in charge?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, you don't know. You don't know whether there was a conversation, you do not know who would have informed Mr. Lukic.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I don't know. I don't know.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you. Mr. Jordash.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: I would like to address you at some stage about the translation of this document and request a verification for various reasons, but I don't think I need to do that before the witness is -- has left.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Unless it creates problems in the questioning of the witness, of course. Then --

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: No, it won't. I'm not going to revisit the subject.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Okay. Then we can do it later.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Apart from that specific purpose, were the -- was your service, the Serbian DB, collecting intelligence for any other purpose?

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Sorry, which service in the Republika Srpska did the post have contact with?

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So what about the military service? Did the State Security Service of Serbia have any contacts with the military service from the point of establish -- from the point the post was established?

utterances.speaker: RADENKO NOVAKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Not that I know of.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So no assistance from the Serbian DB to the military as far as you were aware?

utterances.speaker: RADENKO NOVAKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. I'm a member of a civilian structure. Throughout my career, I was oriented towards civilian structures in Republika Srpska, and I believe the contacts were also at the state level between the RDB of Serbia and the RDB of Republika Srpska. Even during my stay throughout, I have avoided all public appearances.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you. I think that's clear. Could I just ask you about Kozara. Do you know anything about that?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Could I ask one question which is specifically on Bijeljina, so before you move on. When you set up this post in December 1995, after Dayton, did you create -- did you newly establish that post, or did you use an existing facility?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] We used a pre-existing building that we just leased.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I'm not primarily thinking in terms of building, but mainly in terms of equipment, listening equipment.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] That was new. We equipped the facility.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: You came to the building with new equipment, and you established, after Dayton, in December 1995 a listening post in Bijeljina with that new equipment; is that correctly understood?

utterances.speaker: RADENKO NOVAKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Please proceed, Mr. Jordash.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I just want to ask you about Kozara and whether you know anything about DB involvement there, DB of Serbia's involvement there.

utterances.speaker: RADENKO NOVAKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: For a while I believe there was a radio reconnaissance centre in that area, but I'm not sure. I don't know.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Do you know when?

utterances.speaker: RADENKO NOVAKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Maybe in the same years when I was there in 1995, 1996.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Jordash, "maybe" answers, maybe yes, maybe no, is --

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: I know --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: -- I was to -- just about to clarify.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I'm not going to push you. If you don't know, you don't know. Do you have any other information besides what you've just given us about Kozara and the DB's involvement there? I don't want you to guess or speculate. Just if you have facts --

utterances.speaker: RADENKO NOVAKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, no.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you. No further questions. Thank you, Mr. Novakovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Jordash. Mr. Weber, no need for further questions?

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: That's correct, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Mr. Novakovic, the parties have no further questions for you. I've got one question. Questioned by the Court:

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: What exactly was your mission between early July 1995 up till the 5th or the 6th of August, 1995, in the Krajina? What were you doing there?

utterances.speaker: RADENKO NOVAKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: From the beginning of July until early August 1995, I was in Krajina, together with the representatives of the RDB of Serbian Krajina, to be in contact with the security organs of Western Bosnia, Fikret Abdic, for the purpose of collecting intelligence that would be of importance for the security of the Republic of Serbian Krajina.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: What kind of intelligence were you trying to gather at that moment?

utterances.speaker: RADENKO NOVAKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Information related to the deployment of military forces, the 5th Corps, their movements, et cetera, because the situation was getting complicated at the time. There were threats. The Croatian offensive and the Muslim offensive were in the making, threatening an attack against Krajina.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. So if I understand you well, that gathering intelligence would include gathering intelligence of a military nature?

utterances.speaker: RADENKO NOVAKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, there was military intelligence also.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Did you in any way work together with military intelligence -- intelligence services? Because you said, "Well, we were strictly civilian." You earlier emphasised how much that you were always working in the civilian organisation and you were sent to the Krajina apparently to gather intelligence which you just explained was - that's the only thing you mentioned - was, rather, troop movements and these kind of things.

utterances.speaker: RADENKO NOVAKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I worked exclusively with civilian services and I talked with the mediation of the service of the Serbian Krajina with the security forces from AP Western Bosnia, but I never worked with any -- anyone from the military or the military service, with the Military Intelligence Service.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you for that answer. If there are no further questions, Mr. Novakovic, I'd like to thank you very much for coming back in a different season -- Yes, we first move into open session.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: We're in open session, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you, Madam Registrar. I think we should have moved into open session earlier, but ... Mr. Novakovic, I would like to thank you very much for coming again to The Hague and to having answered the questions that were put to you by the parties and by the Bench, and I wish you again a safe return home. You may follow the usher.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [No interpretation]

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: There are two matters I would like to deal with, and I'll inquire with the parties how much time that would take. The first one is the scheduling of a housekeeping session. The Chamber wants to have a housekeeping session on Thursday, the 7th of June, that's one week from now, at 9.00 in the morning. Any problems with that?

utterances.speaker: MS. MARCUS
utterances.text: No problems, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: No problems, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Simatovic Defence?

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, Your Honour, it's okay.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Then there's another matter, that is, the Prosecution would wish to make further submissions in relation to the motion in which it seeks further Browne materials, if I may say. So we're not talking about rebuttal evidence, not about the expert report the Prosecution would like to present in rebuttal to the Browne report, but rather to receive the material and the information. I think the last we heard was that you, Mr. Jordash, you intended to seek Mr. Browne's co-operation so as not to issue an order on that matter. I also do understand that there are some problems in that context. I wonder -- the Prosecution would like to make further submissions in answering to the response by the Defence. I wonder, however, whether we should first take a break and then hear those submissions or whether they would be of such -- so short that we could continue. And I'm specifying address you, Mr. Jordash and Mr. Stanisic.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: Well, my suspicion is that they won't be that short, because I think the -- the -- the issue is --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Then perhaps we take a break first.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: And could I also just raise two other things.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: Very quickly. One is the issue of the translation which I mentioned in relation --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: -- to this document. And the second is just an inquiry as to whether we will be asked to address you on the timing of the filing of the closing briefs.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, you've asked for a postponement of that. I suggest that there's too much on the agenda to deal with it and then adjourn, so let's first take a break. We resume at 20 minutes to 1.00. And could you tell us how much time you would need for the submissions in relation to the Browne materials.

utterances.speaker: MS. MARCUS
utterances.text: Your Honour, from our end, unless there are further queries, about five minutes for the Browne issue and perhaps a little bit more than that for the final trial brief deadline issue.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Then we'll hear from you after the break.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Since it was announced that the submissions in relation to Browne would be most likely the shorter ones, let's start with that. The Prosecution has asked for an opportunity to make submissions, but perhaps it would be good for the Chamber to be updated on the present situation, because I think the last thing we heard in court was that Mr. Jordash would be in contact with Mr. Browne.

utterances.speaker: MS. MARCUS
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour. This is directly in response to that --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. MARCUS
utterances.text: -- so it will all be clear from the submission, and I'm going to ask Ms. Friedman to make that submission for you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Unless there's anything you with like to update on -- us on first, Mr. Jordash.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: Yes, please, because we received an e-mail today at 12.06 from Mr. Browne, who states: "I have just been through all my notes. No pages were detached during my examination other than the book 16 in my report. That is the book that it was always going to be difficult, loads of detached pages when I saw it in March, loads of detached pages when I saw it in November --" No, I'm missing out some bits because they're not strictly relevant, although I'm happy to disclose the full e-mail, if necessary.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: If you tell us what is relevant, then if you perhaps disclose the whole of the e-mail to the Prosecution, then that would ...

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: "Two pages became detached during my examination and were noted and reported as such. The Prosecution have -- already have all those notes. By the way, it was made quite clear during the planning for my examination that the NFI supervisors were the Prosecutor's agents. Did the Prosecution not get a report from them about all of this? If not, what was the point?" And that's it for the moment, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Prosecutor's agents seems to be a rather ambiguous expression.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: Well, I think I understand Mr. Browne, who is saying, "Well, I thought that I was being [indiscernible] for this precise purpose, which is that the NFI observers would make a report concerning the way in which the examination was conducted, including any perceived mishandling or damage, and that report would be sent to the Prosecution." I think that's what he's trying to say. Whether "Prosecutor's agent" is the right words, I -- well, it's -- I think it's probably a bit overstating it, but I think the point is -- is clear.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Then, Ms. Friedman.

utterances.speaker: MS. FRIEDMAN
utterances.text: Yes. Leaving aside for the moment the issue of the NFI, although I can address that, our concern is that Mr. Browne has only been asked to provide information as -- that he -- if there's any additional damage, but our end and as the Defence has indicated, they were going to ask him for only that information which is only part of what our motion requested. They indicated that the rest of the material is irrelevant. The Prosecution disagrees, and we consider all of the material requested to be relevant. And without going into details at this stage, we submit that the response contains inaccuracies, that it repeats arguments that we have responded to when the Defence sought to compel the production of the Mladic notebooks in the courtroom. And our filing of the 22nd of February, 2012, did respond directly to the arguments which are again found in this latest motion. What the motion does not do is address the crux of the Prosecution's position that the Prosecution and the Chamber are entitled to the material which Mr. Browne acknowledged during his testimony should have been put in his report and should have been disclosed. And finally, it should be noted that the Stanisic Defence initially claimed in its e-mail communication that the material was protected by work product. Now apparently because they're unable to support that claim, they indicate that it's irrelevant. And under these circumstances the Prosecution requests that the motion be decided upon, unless the Stanisic Defence requests all of the notes and all of the photographs from Mr. Browne.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Jordash.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: If I may just reply briefly. Firstly, the Prosecution have not addressed the salient issues. A number of issues remain completely unaddressed, including what protocol was used during the time when Milovanovic handled the books, including what steps the Prosecution have taken to establish the protocol that was used by the Serbian MUP when transporting the books to their archives, including what protocol was used during the transport of the books to The Hague at the behest of the Prosecution. And I'll give just one example in relation to what remains unanswered. In the Prosecution's response to our motion to compel the production of the notebooks, the date of their response being the 22nd of February, 2012, the Prosecution indicated that bringing the Mladic notebooks into a carpeted room would itself break the DNA protocol, yet the Prosecution have not indicated whether the room, in relation to when Milovanovic examined those books, was carpeted or not. These are the questions the Prosecution have continued to disregard, in our submission. And at the same time, wanting their cake and eating it, in our submission, they want to now put the Defence to standards which they're not willing to accede to them themselves, by, at the very least, responding to some of these very real concerns. Secondly, whether Mr. Browne acknowledged notes should be disclosed or not is beside the point. It's a legal issue. Mr. Browne is not a lawyer. And thirdly, the issue of whether the Defence object on the basis of relevance or work product, we object on the basis of both. But we have given the Prosecution the relevant information, the relevant information being that the notes do not relate to -- or the remainder of the notes do not relate to the Prosecution's concern about damage, because, as Mr. Browne has confirmed, none of the notes, remaining notes, deal with that subject. The photographs certainly do not deal with that subject. It's very difficult to understand why Mr. Browne's photographs are relevant to that subject at all. And obviously the issue of work product doesn't arise unless the Prosecution establish relevance. They are work product in the absence of --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Jordash, to give a long explanation as to relevance and then to say, well, it's work product anyhow, that's -- is that a very practical approach?

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: Well, I'm just dealing with both points. I think that they're not relevant to the Prosecution's concerns about damage to the notebooks, and in some way the issue of relevance relates to work product.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: But isn't it true that if it's work product, it should not be disclosed whether it's relevant or not?

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: Well, I could see where work product would have to be or perhaps would fall to be disclosed if they became relevant.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mm -- okay.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: In this instance, I think that the two are the flip side of the coin. If Mr. Browne's notes did contain further evidence of damage, then I think to claim work product would be difficult, because they are relevant, then, to an issue before the Court. But in the absence of any of the notes or the photographs being relevant to the issue of damage, we do assert work product and say they're not for the Prosecution or the Court.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Ms. Friedman, any need to respond?

utterances.speaker: MS. FRIEDMAN
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour. Thank you. First, as to the allegations that the Defence says we have not responded to, we have indeed. As I mentioned, in our motion of the 22nd of February, we explained at -- in relation to Manojlo Milovanovic, at paragraph 18 that he was shown originals of the 2008 notebooks for which there is no DNA protocol in place. And in addition to that: When he later dealt with the 2010 notebooks, he reviewed the electronic copies. This is also the reason that they were scanned when they came to the OTP, another assertion that was made, although not orally now but in the response, that the Prosecution not explain the need to scan it, and we did so in paragraph 16 of the 22nd of February filing, because the copies were not of high enough quality that they could be used and we would have had to constantly use the notebook, so we had to take high-quality electronic, colour scans that would be complete and could be used in the future. And with respect to the issue of the protocol that existed, this is again addressed in paragraph 17 of the 22nd of February filing, where we explained that we used a clean-room protocol which included blocking air vents, cleaning the room, scanner, and equipment with a particular chemical provided by the NFI. Cleaning the surfaces between the processing of groups of evidence and requiring staff members entering the room to swear surgical masks, soft nitrile examination gloves, and full protection suits. I'm sorry to repeat this now, but since the allegations do keep arising, it's important for us to put on the record that there is -- there's only been an attempt by the Prosecution to maintain as best as possible the condition of these notebooks to prevent further deterioration, especially when -- under circumstances where it's unnecessary. And the Prosecution did provide the notebooks to be examined on two occasions under a strict protocol because of the efforts that are being made in order to maintain that evidence. Now, as for Mr. Browne's acknowledgement being -- him being unable to legally explain, the issue is that when he in court was asked about items and said, "This should have been in my report," we see that his report is incomplete. And at this stage it is a little late to now ask him what else -- asking him the specific question of whether additional pages were damaged is not the pertinent question at this stage. What's been demonstrated is that what needed to be in his report was not in his report. His notes, I would ask Mr. Jordash to articulate what the work product concern is, because there doesn't seem to be any articulation of that in the Rules of this Tribunal or even in common law jurisprudence how it is that the notes of a witness about the evidence itself and not about Defence strategy or communication with the Defence would be work product. Moreover, it would be -- it would have been broken when it was -- when part of them were already displayed, when there was no objection previously, when they were discussed, when they were offered. So I would like to just ask what the basis for the work product claim is.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: That's it. Mr. Jordash, briefly, could I ask you also specifically, apart from the work-product question put to you by Ms. Friedman, what is exactly -- to what extent does the one request, that is, to be further informed about what happened, how does that influence the decision on the motion? I mean, the Prosecution is seeking something, and you say, Yes, but you've provided us with insufficient information about what happened before. Now, I can imagine, of course, you have -- you have made a -- of course you have to have sought the protection of the books, but to what extent is -- I hardly dare to say -- is the tu quoque reasoning applicable in these procedural circumstances? To say, You should deny the motion because the Prosecution has not given us the relevant information we need.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: Well, first of all, because it goes to the merits of their position. They take scans of these documents on two separate occasions. It is -- it's difficult to -- to accept that that scanning process does not damage any of these books whatsoever, that somehow Mr. Browne under a strict protocol damaged one of the books but the Prosecution's scanning of the books on two occasions didn't damage anything. Now, the Prosecution want Mr. Browne's notes. Where are the notes that the Prosecution must have taken if they're going to demand of the Defence what they've lived up to themselves? And so --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Sorry to interrupt you. Have you asked whether any notes were taken by the Prosecution and have you invited them to produce them?

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: We've asked for any and all information relating to the treatment of these books since they were seized by the Serbian MUP authorities.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: Including protocols. We've had no disclosure of any of these so-called protocols the Prosecution say they have in place.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: And --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Ms. Friedman, perhaps, because -- sorry to shortcut, but I would like to be it a debate [sic]. Is there any reason why you wouldn't disclose to the Defence the protocols which apparently you've used?

utterances.speaker: MS. FRIEDMAN
utterances.text: Your Honours, you've -- you -- you -- the same way you asked the relevance, that's our question. If we've asserted, as officers of the court, we've explained what it is that we're doing to protect them, and the suspicion and the aspersions are not really -- we don't understand the basis of it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Okay. Let's try to be very practical. The protocols you say you've used, but there may be a confusion about what a protocol is. Was it put on paper?

utterances.speaker: MS. FRIEDMAN
utterances.text: We can --

utterances.speaker: MS. FRIEDMAN
utterances.text: We can -- we can investigate further with the OTP Evidence Unit, but in terms of -- if I could just add --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: No, no. I'd like to keep matters at this moment. You may add whatever you want at a later stage. So, what happened, as a matter of fact, is that Mr. Jordash asked you about what protocols were applied, and then you gave some rules which apparently were applied without even having thought about whether these rules were ever put on paper and -- because, having no answer. It's clear that the protocol for the inspection of the notebooks by Mr. Browne, I think they were negotiated for half a year, and so they are on paper. Would -- would you -- if there's any written protocol, would you give it to Mr. Jordash?

utterances.speaker: MS. FRIEDMAN
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Mr. Jordash, therefore, if it exists, you'll have access to it. And if not, you'll give to the best of your abilities the details of what rules applied at all stages of the seizure and later transportation and handling of these materials. Is that ...

utterances.speaker: MS. FRIEDMAN
utterances.text: Yeah, we can provide that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Jordash, I didn't ask these questions from the Prosecution. I'm a bit surprised that the Prosecution only now starts thinking about whether there's a written document on the protocols, yes or not, because that -- I would have expected this to be dealt with earlier in the discussion between the parties. I asked it before because I think that just as the Prosecution is seeking the best available information about what happened and -- and exactly that you should be entitled to have the same information, not to say that if one party doesn't apply the same rules as the other, that that necessarily means that -- that the parties should give up their claim on gaining information. It's not matter of, as they say in Latin, "do ut des," "I give it to you, so you give it to me." I mean, it's not an exchange. There's a motion by the Prosecution. And I'm seeking whether the information you say you need, again, whether that's a reason -- not to counter-motion is a different matter, but whether you would be informed as fully as possible. And the Prosecution are -- is finding out whether at least there are any written protocols available.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Okay. So we have the protocols. Any more to be said about the protocols?

utterances.speaker: MS. FRIEDMAN
utterances.text: Not strictly on the protocols.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Then any -- I interrupted you, Mr. Jordash, in order to see whether we could make any progress on a certain matter. I would like, then to give you the floor again to further proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: I'm not sure there's anything I'd like to add other than to -- to reiterate the point about the notes. We would find it more -- less objectionable to be asked for notes if the Prosecution had kept notes themselves when handling the notebooks.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Simple question: Have notes been made?

utterances.speaker: MS. FRIEDMAN
utterances.text: Yes, they have, but, Your Honours, this is really besides the point because we have provided the information --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: My question simply was whether notes were made. Next question: Are you willing to share these notes with the Defence?

utterances.speaker: MS. FRIEDMAN
utterances.text: Yes, we are.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Jordash, equality has been finally established in this respect. Or is -- The answer was "yes," Ms. Friedman? I see that there was some further conversation within the Prosecution, but I've not heard that the answer has changed. So notes are -- now you may proceed. I interrupted you again - --

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: No, I mean, if the Prosecution are willing to disclose the notes that they've made which relate to their handling of the books, and I mean, when I use the word "notes," the notes which should reflect whether any damage has been done to the books by their handling.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: What notes should reflect is different from what notes reflect. You can ask for notes that do exist. The Prosecution is not asking any more than notes that are in existence. And whether the notes that should have contained other information than they actually contain is a different matter. But could I say that you would expect to read in those notes how the material was handled?

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: And whether any -- yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Okay. So the Prosecution, as far as I understand, gives the written protocols to the extent they exist. They give, as best -- to the best of their abilities, information about anything, what happened during their handling, give that information. And if any notes exist on that matter, they'll be disclosed to the Prosecution -- to the Defence as well. Have I summarised the situation?

utterances.speaker: MS. FRIEDMAN
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Mr. Jordash, I think we made one or two steps forward. Does this in any way influence your -- because it was part of your argument why it would be unfair to ask Mr. Browne to provide what the Prosecution is seeking.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: Yes. I mean, of course it does influence my -- but let me just -- if I can just take one step back, which is to say this: That the issue before the Court, or certainly one of the issues in relation to the Mladic notebooks, is the source of the damage to the notebooks, and in particular the book, I think book 16, which most, on one view, implicates Mr. Stanisic. And -- I mean, we -- we are concerned that if -- this issue has been before the Court for some time. We've made it very clear. And what I'm concerned about is now hearing from the Prosecution, if I take what they say on face value that they have notes relating to or potentially relating to this issue, why it is, if they're acting in good faith, why it is those notes have not been disclosed previous to today.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: But I'm raising that now because what I'm mindful of is that we make a concession, and I'm minded to make that concession that we should disclose Mr. Browne's notes, and then what we get from the Prosecution is another kind of note which just shows some kind of broad-brush continuity rather than an examination.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I expect the Prosecution to disclose the notes they have on this matter. And -- and whether they are good notes or bad notes or -- that is -- we can't force a party to disclose notes that do not exist.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: We can instruct the party, order a party, to provide information as fully as possible, and as officers of the court they have to meet such an order. If there is any material. If a party says, "We're willing to disclose these notes," then I expect them to disclose the notes, all of them as they are in existence, dealing with this matter. And further suspicions about not being loyal in that respect are for the next stage, I would say. Mr. Groome.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Your Honour, simply to say the Prosecution accepts that the -- and we will undertake to provide notes. I was under the impression that they had been provided, and I didn't come today having fully refreshed my recollection, but I do recall the evidence log, the notes of every movement of that book, being provided to the Defence. But I will check that and I will make sure that Mr. Jordash is provided with all notes related to the book. But I think I want to make the point here that what the Prosecution is interested in is whether the books sustained additional damage during Mr. Browne's examination upon which he then made a conclusion based upon damage that he may himself have caused. The Prosecution have very clear in its -- in its questioning of Dr. Browne that we accepted that the books were damaged, and we were unable to say with any great certainty how much damage was caused by the recovery by the Serb police or how much damage was caused prior to the recovery by the police. But I think the relevant issue for us is whether or not we accept Dr. Browne's assessment of what damage the condition was in when he received them. We just want to know what additional damage. And that was prompted by the inadvertent disclosure of one of his notes where he had written "I have damaged the notebooks." So we just want to be clear about what damage was caused by his examination.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Let's -- let's -- at this moment it seems that the parties have moved closer to each other.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: In relation to the disclosure of the notes, I don't think we have. And the reason for that --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Okay, but let's not discuss it now. Mr. Groome will check it, what you have received, and then you may further discuss it. If you say, "Isn't -- isn't this available or isn't that available," Mr. Groome - and that's at least how I understand the position of the Prosecution - committed himself to provide every note on paper made which deals with the handling of the books prior to the examination of Mr. Browne.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Your Honour, and could I add something: It is confirming my recollection. I'm just receiving an e-mail that we have provided all of the material that we have - OTP staff declarations; the evidence registration logs and movement logs; as well as we made the investigator who was given responsibility for handling the books, Ms. Erin Gallagher, available for an interview by the Defence so they could fully explore this issue. We've also provided all of the Serbian MUP reports that we received in relation to this. So I can confirm that my recollection was correct that we have provided everything we have. I will double-check whether, since this disclosure was made, whether there's any additional material, but all this material has been provided.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: This is why -- this is why we're going round and round in circles, because what I'm talking -- I accept. I've accepted that for a long time that the Prosecution, in Mr. Groome's customary open way, has disclosed these documents. What he hasn't disclosed is whether there was a concerted effort to record the -- the state of the books before the scanning, the damage done to the books during the scanning, ditto during Milovanovic's examination, and so on. These are the types of notes that they're requesting from the Defence, and these are the types of notes, it would appear, they have not kept themselves.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: If they do not exist any more, then of course it's impossible to produce them now. Have you used the offer to interview - who was it? - so to --

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: But it -- that doesn't help, because we have, and that was again typical of Mr. Groome to make that available. But -- or her available. But she doesn't know -- in the absence of keeping detailed notes, she cannot tell us page 16 out of 1.050 was damaged or not damaged at a given time. It's that material. So the Prosecution stand to gain our notes and say, "Look, you've damaged," and by not keeping the notes themselves --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: No, I mean, they would like to know. If --

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: Well, we would like to know.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Hm?

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: Sorry, Your Honour. We would like to know what damage the Prosecution --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: -- did to the books.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Of course. If it would not have been written down, the Prosecution wouldn't know either. Of course. Our sources of knowledge are limited to what exists and what is in the minds of persons we can ask for, but let me not take it any further at this moment. Let me just confer with my colleagues.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: The Chamber is assisted by the submissions and will decide on the matter. Then, next item was final briefs. Mr. Jordash, you go first?

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: Oh, do I have to?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: No. It was a line with a question mark. It is quarter past 1.00. We have half an hour available. Who goes first and how is the time divided?

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: Your Honour --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: And is the Simatovic Defence claiming the same time, or have you consulted with Mr. Jordash? Does he present the position of both Defence?

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: Your Honours, we consulted with Mr. Jordash and we will take the same position.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Who goes first?

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: I wondering -- sorry to interrupt.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: I wonder if I might just make a two-minute application for verification of the translation of --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, yes. You announced that earlier. Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: Well, I can deal with it in two minutes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Please do so.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: P3169, to my mind, from the English, translation is ambiguous. It's ambiguous because in the first paragraph it uses the phrase "I met up at the hotel," which could indicate a casual -- a casual pass-by, if you like, or it could indicate a meeting.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: The second paragraph, "I encountered the same group," appearing to reflect a similar type of passing-by or meeting as the first paragraph, which suggests a much more brief meeting. The word "encounter" in this context, in my submission, suggest something a bit more casual. The Prosecution's interpretation is of something very definite: a meeting. The Defence position is that "encounter," or something looser like that, is a much more natural interpretation. So perhaps, in our view, an attempt by the Translation Unit to look at this would assist the Court.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Apart from the linguistic aspect, of course, linguistic aspect is one of the aspects in interpreting the content of documents, as long as the parties are aware of that, I think it might be good to have it verified whether --

utterances.speaker: MS. MARCUS
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour, we didn't want to interrupt but we --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. MARCUS
utterances.text: -- share the concern and we will submit it for verification.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Okay. With these -- those specific questions attached to the request.

utterances.speaker: MS. MARCUS
utterances.text: Absolutely, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you, Ms. Marcus. Then, who goes first with the final briefs?

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: I'm happy to make some brief submissions.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Please do so.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: We would request until the end of September for the filing of the closing brief, give or take a few -- or one or two weeks, depending upon when the evidence finishes. If the Court witness is called and takes the time that would look likely, then we may not finish the evidence until late in June, and we would submit a three-month period for a closing brief following a case of this size and complexity is not unreasonable. I'm not going to address in detail size. Your Honours have sat on several cases and will have in mind, no doubt, the size of this case in relation to other cases, but it is a sizable indictment, a broad indictment with a wide-ranging joint criminal enterprise alleged. Complexity is a bit more at the heart of our concern. This is not the type of case which involves a large swathe of evidence which can be safely put to the side as unimportant or agreed testimony. The -- the contentious issues in this case really range from the crime-base evidence, for example, whether -- and what -- what Martic's Police were doing in the Krajina, for example, or what Mijovic may have been doing in Bratunac, we have to go right to the ground, all the way to the Prosecution allegation that Mr. Stanisic played some kind of quasi-political role. So we have to go right to the top to consider the role of the top leadership from Croatia, Bosnia, and Belgrade. So we really do have, in our submission, an extremely complicated case where the issues range from top to bottom, but also which is reflected in the kind of focus which has to be played -- which has to be given to the evidence. In our submission, much turns on the detailed examination of hundreds, if not thousands, of exhibits. For example, in our submission, if one puts side by side the exhibits which deal with the Bratunac Red Berets, Your Honours will come to the conclusion that the Defence will urge upon you. But only when Your Honours are taken through those exhibits one by one can a chronology be seen and the truth be ascertained. And, in our submission, it's only through the minute examination of many of those exhibits and much of the witness testimony that Your Honours, in our view, will arrive at a just verdict. And, in our submission, a bit more time to write the closing brief will assist Your Honours to arrive at the right verdict and will assist Your Honours in arriving at the right verdict maybe perhaps more quickly than Your Honours would. I think the Prosecution are, I think, a skilled team. We hope that the Defence have -- can rise to that challenge, too, and in doing so, if given a bit more time, provide you with the type of assistance which we submit you would need to be able to arrive at the right verdict. Finally, we had a quick e-mail exchange with a few Defence teams yesterday, and we would suggest that the three months that we're effectively asking for would not be unreasonable compared to, for example, the Zupljanin case, which, whilst being granted in the end only five weeks, effectively had from the beginning of the year until May interspersed with a handful of rebuttal witnesses and, prior to that, had September till December of 2011 where they were sitting only two weeks out of every four because of the Haradinaj case. We've been, as Your Honours know, sitting intensely for some time and will do until perhaps the end of June. So it's very difficult to make comparisons, that's what we've found, but nonetheless, we do think that's a useful comparison. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. If comparisons are to be made, it should be as broad as possible so that it really gives a full overview. That's --

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: Well, perhaps I can just throw in, if I may, and Her Honour Judge Picard will correct me if I'm wrong, but the Perisic case, the parties were given, I think, six weeks after the last Status Conference of the 2nd of May, 2012. In our submission, that case was significantly less complex in the way that it focused on one accused and focused on largely the supplying from one entity to another as compared to this, which -- this case, which involves a multitude of types of supplies to various locations.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I think, as a matter of fact, that a comparison is -- it's a complex matter.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Because every case has its own specific features and a variety of -- of elements to consider, and the Chamber, of course, will carefully consider the comparisons you made. Mr. Petrovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, with your leave, just two sentences. Our Defence team supports everything that our learned friend Mr. Jordash said. We only wish to emphasise two circumstances that may bring about a considerable change to the hitherto case record in this trial. The witness the Court intends to call and the evidence in the form of personnel files that the Prosecution intends to present in their rebuttal case, those two circumstances that will come to light by the end of June bring about a tectonic change to the case record so far. Any kind of work we may do now, without having a clear idea of how that will end, would be futile. As things stand now, three weeks after the leading of that evidence can certainly not be sufficient for the work that we need to be done to be done well. And if you allow me just one more thing. After having done a preliminary analysis of everything that should be included in the closing brief, our preliminary position is that the limit of 60.000 words will not be enough, and we will have to apply to the Trial Chamber to modify that limit. And we will attempt to do so, as our colleague Mr. Jordash has indicated.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Petrovic. Prosecution.

utterances.speaker: MS. MARCUS
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour. The Prosecution appreciates the Chamber's offer to the parties to make submissions regarding the proposed deadline for final trial briefs. The Prosecution notes that it will strive to meet any deadline set by the Chamber. We wish to express our concern at the difficulty which the Prosecution will likely face in driving to meet the proposed pre-summer recess deadline for completion of the final trial brief. The Prosecution requests that the deadline for final submissions be set at the 31st of August, a six-week extension of the Chamber's previously announced deadline, for the following reasons: The purpose of final submissions is to allow the parties to assist the Chamber to the greatest extent possible in the examination of the evidence and the search for the truth. Decisions related to the timing of final briefs must, in our submission, be informed primarily by that goal. Of course, expediency is an important interest as well, but we submit that given the length and complexity of the trial, the time that we seek in order to devote exclusively to the preparation of the brief is reasonable. We submit that the interests of justice are best served by the Prosecution and the Defence having developed carefully considered and carefully crafted final submissions. Your Honours, the reasonableness of the extension sought by the parties must be assessed in light of three factors: The first factor is the length of the proceedings. These proceedings have now been ongoing for three years. In this context, a six-week extension of the deadline for the briefs is proportional and reasonable to the benefit to be achieved. The second factor is the extent of the evidentiary record in this case. The record now runs to 20.000 transcript pages and more than 4.000 exhibits, with new materials still being admitted through Defence witnesses and through the bar table. We note in this respect the filing today of the Simatovic Defence in which they foreshadowed a combination of approximately 510 documents they anticipate tendering from the bar table in the future. A period of uninterrupted work following the close of the evidence is required to synthesise and make intelligent arguments regarding a body of evidence of that size. The third factor is the critical importance of final submissions in assisting the Chamber in its fundamental task: the search for truth. This extension is not sought for the completion of a frivolous or peripheral task. It is sought to enable the parties to properly disarming one of their primary duties in this case. In light of these considerations, a six-week extension is, in our submission, entirely appropriate. The Prosecution finds itself with limited resources at this stage of the proceedings. All but one of the attorneys on the Stanisic/Simatovic Prosecution team is engaged on two cases. As the Chamber is aware, the time-period prior to the summer recess will involve a confluence of competing and urgent matters, all of which are central to the Prosecution's obligations. We have been working steadily on the brief for the past two months. Nonetheless, the rebuttal filings, bar table responses, witness preparation, and housekeeping, and now the response to the motion filed earlier this week by the Stanisic Defence, all are critical tasks being undertaken by the Prosecution team, which have effectively prevented us from spending the time necessary to progress our closing submissions. Under these circumstances, the Prosecution agrees with the Defence that the interests of justice are not served by the filing of the final briefs prior to the summer recess. The Prosecution appreciates this opportunity, and we are ready to meet any instructions issued by the Chamber in this regard. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: May I take it that there's no need to respond to what seems to be a concurring position by the parties. Then we adjourn. And we'll resume on Thursday, the 7th of June, at 9.00 in the morning in this -- yes, Mr. -- I --

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: Sorry, could -- just very quickly -- could the accused be excused in the customary way from the housekeeping session?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: From the housekeeping sessions. If -- it almost goes without saying. If Mr. Stanisic and/or Mr. Simatovic think they can use their time better and more pleasant, then they're excused.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: So therefore, I was interrupted when I said the 7th of June, at 9.00 in the morning, in this same courtroom, II.
